enonce_markdown:
A trolley is released on a gentle slope in a school laboratory. A sensor gives these readings of its velocity.

| Time / s | 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 |

What is the acceleration of the trolley?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$. Check that the change of velocity is the same in equal time intervals (uniform acceleration).

### Solution

The velocity rises by $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in every $4\,\mathrm{s}$, so the acceleration is uniform:

$a = \dfrac{6 - 0}{12 - 0} = \dfrac{6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}{12\,\mathrm{s}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (option **a**).

- Option b is $\dfrac{\Delta t}{\Delta v} = \dfrac{4}{2}$ (inverted fraction).
- Option c is the final velocity, not the rate of change.
- Option d is the final time.

enonce_markdown:
A motorcyclist rides along a straight road. His velocity is recorded every $10$ seconds.

| Time / s | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 |

Which one of the following correctly describes his motion and the distance travelled in $40\,\mathrm{s}$?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity (zero acceleration). The distance travelled is the area under the graph: for a rectangle, $s = v \times t$.

### Solution

The velocity never changes, so the motion is at **constant velocity** ($a = 0$).

$s = v \times t = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \times 40\,\mathrm{s} = 400\,\mathrm{m}$ (option **c**).

- Option a confuses the value of the velocity with an acceleration; the acceleration is $0$.
- Option b divides the time by the velocity ($40 \div 10$) instead of multiplying.
- Option d is wrong: a velocity of $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is not rest.

enonce_markdown:
A lorry travels along a straight road. Its velocity at different times is given below, and between these times the velocity changes at a steady rate.

| Time / s | 0 | 10 | 30 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 0 | 20 | 20 | 0 |

What total distance does the lorry travel in the $40\,\mathrm{s}$?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The distance travelled is the area under the velocity-time graph. Split the graph into simple shapes (triangles and a rectangle) and add their areas.

### Solution

The graph has three parts:

- $0$ to $10\,\mathrm{s}$ (speeding up): triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100\,\mathrm{m}$;
- $10$ to $30\,\mathrm{s}$ (constant velocity, $20\,\mathrm{s}$ long): rectangle, $20 \times 20 = 400\,\mathrm{m}$;
- $30$ to $40\,\mathrm{s}$ (slowing down): triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100\,\mathrm{m}$.

Total $= 100 + 400 + 100 = 600\,\mathrm{m}$ (option **d**). Check with the trapezium formula: $\tfrac{1}{2}(20 + 40) \times 20 = 600\,\mathrm{m}$.

- Option a counts only the two triangles and forgets the constant-velocity part.
- Option b treats the graph as one triangle of base $30\,\mathrm{s}$.
- Option c counts only the constant-velocity rectangle.

enonce_markdown:
A bus leaves a stop in Douala and travels along a straight road. Its velocity is recorded as follows. Between consecutive readings the velocity changes at a steady rate.

| Time / s | 0 | 8 | 32 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 0 | 16 | 16 | 0 |

(a) Calculate the acceleration during the first $8\,\mathrm{s}$.

(b) Calculate the deceleration during the last $8\,\mathrm{s}$.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the bus.

(d) Calculate the average speed of the bus for the whole $40\,\mathrm{s}$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On a velocity-time graph: the gradient gives the acceleration, $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$; the area under the graph gives the distance; average speed $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$.

### Solution

(a) $a = \dfrac{16 - 0}{8 - 0} = 2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

(b) $a = \dfrac{0 - 16}{40 - 32} = -2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so the deceleration is $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) Area under the graph:

- speeding up: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 16 = 64\,\mathrm{m}$;
- constant velocity (from $8\,\mathrm{s}$ to $32\,\mathrm{s}$, i.e. $24\,\mathrm{s}$): $24 \times 16 = 384\,\mathrm{m}$;
- slowing down: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 16 = 64\,\mathrm{m}$.

Total $= 64 + 384 + 64 = 512\,\mathrm{m}$.

(d) Average speed $= \dfrac{512\,\mathrm{m}}{40\,\mathrm{s}} = 12.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (less than the maximum $16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, as expected, because of the starting and stopping).

enonce_markdown:
A car on a straight road in Bamenda slows down steadily. Its velocity is measured at four times.

| Time / s | 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 24 | 18 | 12 | 6 |

The car continues to slow down at the same rate until it stops. What distance does the car travel from $t = 0$ until it stops?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Find the acceleration from the gradient, use it to find when the velocity reaches zero, and then take the area under the graph from $t = 0$ to that moment (a triangle).

### Solution

Gradient: $a = \dfrac{18 - 24}{4} = -1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (the same in every interval).

Time to stop: $24 - 1.5\,t = 0$, so $t = 16\,\mathrm{s}$.

Distance = area of the triangle with base $16\,\mathrm{s}$ and height $24\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:

$s = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 24 = 192\,\mathrm{m}$ (option **b**).

- Option a is the distance travelled up to $t = 12\,\mathrm{s}$ only ($\tfrac{1}{2}(24 + 6) \times 12 = 180\,\mathrm{m}$).
- Option c is the rectangle $24 \times 12$, which ignores the slowing down.
- Option d is the rectangle $24 \times 16$, the distance if the car did not slow down.

enonce_markdown:
A train leaves a station, travels at a steady speed and then brakes to stop at the next station. Between consecutive readings its velocity changes at a steady rate.

| Time / s | 0 | 12 | 40 | 55 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 0 | 18 | 18 | 0 |

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the train in the first $12\,\mathrm{s}$.

(b) Calculate the deceleration during braking.

(c) Calculate the distance between the two stations.

(d) Calculate the distance travelled by the train in the last $5\,\mathrm{s}$ before it stops.

(e) At what time is the velocity of the train $9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while it is braking?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Gradient of a velocity-time graph = acceleration; area under it = distance. During uniform braking the velocity decreases linearly, so the velocity at any instant can be found from the deceleration.

### Solution

(a) $a = \dfrac{18 - 0}{12 - 0} = 1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

(b) Braking lasts $55 - 40 = 15\,\mathrm{s}$: $a = \dfrac{0 - 18}{15} = -1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, a deceleration of $1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) Distance = total area under the graph:

- $0$ to $12\,\mathrm{s}$: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 18 = 108\,\mathrm{m}$;
- $12$ to $40\,\mathrm{s}$: $28 \times 18 = 504\,\mathrm{m}$;
- $40$ to $55\,\mathrm{s}$: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 18 = 135\,\mathrm{m}$.

Total $= 108 + 504 + 135 = 747\,\mathrm{m}$.

(d) At $t = 50\,\mathrm{s}$ the velocity is $18 - 1.2 \times 10 = 6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The last $5\,\mathrm{s}$ form a triangle:

$s = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 6 = 15\,\mathrm{m}$.

(e) During braking $v = 18 - 1.2\,(t - 40)$. Setting $v = 9$: $t - 40 = \dfrac{18 - 9}{1.2} = 7.5\,\mathrm{s}$, so $t = 47.5\,\mathrm{s}$ (half-way in velocity, but not half-way in distance).
